texts.firmware.a52bios.about: The Atari 5200's boot ROM. It must be exactly 2048 bytes, and a file of any other size is refused.
texts.firmware.cvbios.about: The ColecoVision's boot ROM (8 KB). It holds the console's title screen and its cartridge checks, and nothing runs without it.
texts.firmware.gbabios.about: The Game Boy Advance's boot ROM (16 KB). The real one is needed. The core runs it, games call functions in it and its timing is part of the machine. It is Nintendo's and you have to supply it.
texts.firmware.gbboot.about: The Game Boy's boot ROM (256 bytes). It scrolls the logo and checks the cartridge. The core runs it and the game starts from the state it leaves, so it is required. It is Nintendo's and you have to supply it. The boot ROM of any original Game Boy revision works. DMG-CPU A is the one ares expects for a plain Game Boy.
texts.firmware.gbcboot.about: The Game Boy Color's boot ROM (2 KB). It is larger than the Game Boy's because it also chooses the colours an original Game Boy cartridge is shown in.
texts.firmware.m32xbootm.about: The boot ROM of the first of the 32X's two SH-2 processors (2 KB).
texts.firmware.m32xboots.about: The boot ROM of the second of the 32X's two SH-2 processors (1 KB).
texts.firmware.m32xvector.about: The 256-byte table the Mega Drive's 68000 processor starts from on a 32X. It is Sega's and you have to supply it. The three 32X files come from the same dump. The letter in each name says which processor runs it: G for the Mega Drive side, M and S for the two SH-2 processors.
texts.firmware.megacdbios.about: The BIOS of the Mega CD disc drive. It is Sega's and you have to supply it. A disc only starts with the BIOS of its own region. A USA game needs the Sega CD BIOS and a Japanese game the Japanese Mega CD BIOS. The Model 1 and Model 2 versions both work. They show a different menu, and games behave the same on both.
texts.firmware.msx2main.about: The MSX2's main ROM (32 KB). It belongs to Microsoft and ASCII, and you have to supply it. An MSX2 also needs its sub ROM.
texts.firmware.msx2sub.about: The MSX2's sub ROM (16 KB). It holds the extended BIOS that the main ROM calls.
texts.firmware.msxbios.about: The MSX's BIOS and BASIC ROM (32 KB). The ROM of any MSX machine works, and they differ by region. The one named here is the one this core was tested with. A project records which one it used.
texts.firmware.n64ddipl.about: The 64DD disk drive's own boot ROM (4 MB). The console starts from it when no cartridge is in, and it reads the disk. It is Nintendo's and you have to supply it. The Japanese IPL is the one the Japanese disks, which are almost all of them, were made for.
texts.firmware.ngbios.about: The boot ROM of the Neo Geo home console (128 KB). The file is `neo-epo.bin`. It is usually found inside an `aes.zip` BIOS set and has to be taken out of the zip first.
texts.firmware.ngpbios.about: The boot ROM of the original black-and-white Neo Geo Pocket (64 KB). Its name usually carries the year 1998, which tells it apart from the Color one.
texts.firmware.ngpcbios.about: The boot ROM of the Neo Geo Pocket Color (64 KB). It is a different ROM from the black-and-white machine's, and one cannot be used in place of the other.
texts.firmware.pcesystemcard.about: The card that goes in the card slot of a CD-ROM2 or a TurboDuo. Without it the machine cannot read a disc. It is NEC's and you have to supply it. A Super CD-ROM2 game needs System Card 3.0 of its region (the Japanese card for a Japanese disc, the American card for a US disc). An early CD-ROM2 game works with any card. A Games Express disc needs the Games Express card. The card shows its name when the machine starts. A disc that stops at PUSH RUN BUTTON usually needs a newer card.
texts.firmware.ps1bios.about: The PlayStation's boot ROM (512 KB). It is the console's operating system. Games call it all the time and nothing runs without it. It is Sony's and you have to supply it. Any retail BIOS works, and they differ by region and revision. The one named here is the one this core was tested with. A project records which one it used.
texts.firmware.sfcipl.about: The 64 bytes the SNES sound processor runs when the console is switched on. The main processor uses them to load sound code, so nothing plays without this file. It is Nintendo's and you have to supply it. Games with an extra chip in the cartridge (the DSP-1 in Pilotwings, the CX4 in Mega Man X2) also need that chip's ROM. This core does not ask for those yet.
texts.firmware.wsboot.about: The WonderSwan's boot ROM. It shows the startup animation, sets the machine up and reads the owner's name from the console's memory.
texts.firmware.wscboot.about: The WonderSwan Color's boot ROM. It is a different file from the WonderSwan's.
texts.firmware.zxsbios.about: The ZX Spectrum's ROM (16 KB). It holds the BASIC language, the editor and the tape loader, so the machine cannot run without it. Amstrad owns it and allows it to be distributed with emulators. This core does not include it, and you have to supply it.
texts.setting.ares.color_emulation.about: Shows the colours the way the console's own screen showed them, and not the raw values as a modern display would show them. It changes the recorded picture.
texts.setting.ares.communication_id.about: The number this machine has when several are linked together.
texts.setting.ares.deep_black_boost.about: Makes the darkest colours darker, as a television showed them. It changes the picture only.
texts.setting.ares.fast_boot.about: Skips the console's boot ROM and starts the game at once. The machine is in a different state when the game starts, so a movie recorded with this on does not play back with it off.
texts.setting.ares.free_play.about: One of the Neo Geo system board's switches. It lets a game start without coins.
texts.setting.ares.freeze.about: One of the Neo Geo system board's switches. On an arcade board it stops the game while it is set.
texts.setting.ares.headphones.about: Whether headphones are plugged in. The console's sound is different with them.
texts.setting.ares.interframe_blending.about: Mixes each frame with the one before it, the way the LCD screens of the time blurred movement. The game runs the same. The recorded picture is different, so a movie's video changes when this is on.
texts.setting.ares.multiplayer.about: One of the Neo Geo system board's switches. It turns on play between linked machines.
texts.setting.ares.normal_controller.about: One of the Neo Geo system board's switches. It tells the system ROM that an ordinary controller is connected, and not a mahjong one.
texts.setting.ares.orientation.about: Which way the handheld is held. Some games are played with it turned on its side.
texts.setting.ares.phosphor.about: Mixes each frame with the one before it, the way a television tube kept its picture for a moment.
texts.setting.ares.ppu1_version.about: The revision number of the first of the console's two video chips. A game can read it.
texts.setting.ares.ppu2_version.about: The revision number of the second of the console's two video chips. A game can read it.
texts.setting.ares.revision.about: Which revision of the console this is. Revisions of the real console behave differently in small ways, and a game that depends on one may act differently on another.
texts.setting.ares.settings_mode.about: One of the Neo Geo system board's switches. On an arcade board it opens the board's own settings screens when the machine starts.
texts.setting.ares.show_icons.about: Draws the handheld's status icons around the picture.
texts.setting.ares.two_coin_chutes.about: One of the Neo Geo system board's switches. It tells the system ROM whether the cabinet has one coin slot or two.
texts.setting.ares.version.about: Which revision of the console this is. Revisions of the real console behave differently in small ways, and a game that depends on one may act differently on another.
texts.setting.ares.vram.about: How much video memory the console has. A real console has 64 KB.
texts.setting.ares_option.about: The %1 option that ares calls "%2". It has no description yet.
texts.setting.bobdeinterlace.about: How an interlaced picture is turned into full frames. On, each field is stretched into a frame of its own (bob). Off, two fields are combined into one frame (weave). It changes the picture only.
texts.setting.fastvi.about: Skips three steps the Nintendo 64 applies to its picture (divot removal, anti-aliasing and gamma). It is faster and the picture looks slightly different. The game runs exactly the same. The setting is saved with the project because it changes how a recorded video looks.
texts.setting.initialtime.about: What the cartridge's clock shows when the machine is switched on, in seconds since 1970 (Unix time). Only a few cartridges have a clock. This is a setting, and not your computer's clock, so that a movie plays back the same on any day.
texts.setting.machine.about: Which console this project is for. Everything else depends on it, so changing it restarts the core.
texts.setting.mcd.bios.about: Which region's Mega CD BIOS to use. A disc only starts with the BIOS of its own region. A USA game needs the Sega CD BIOS, a Japanese game the Japanese Mega CD BIOS and a European game the European one. The Model 1 and Model 2 versions show a different menu, and games behave the same on both.
texts.setting.n64cpu.about: How the Nintendo 64's processors are emulated. The recompiler turns the game's code into code for your computer and is about three times faster. The interpreter runs it one instruction at a time, as this core always did before this setting existed. The two time instructions differently. It is part of the machine, so a movie needs the same value: a project made before this setting existed was made with the interpreter, and plays back only with Interpreter chosen. Changing it restarts the core.
texts.setting.pcecd.card.about: Which System Card is in the card slot. The card is what reads the disc. A Super CD-ROM2 game needs System Card 3.0 of its own region. An early CD-ROM2 game works with any card. A Games Express disc needs the Games Express card. The card shows its name when the machine starts. A disc that stops at PUSH RUN BUTTON usually needs a newer card.
texts.setting.port1.about: What is plugged into the first controller port. 'default' is the device this machine normally has there, and 'none' leaves the port empty. Each of the other choices exists on certain machines only, and choosing one on a machine that does not have it is refused. They are arcadeStick (Neo Geo), controlPad (Mega Drive), controller (Atari 5200), digitalGamepad (PlayStation), ePSM (NES), gamepad (Nintendo 64, NES, Master System, Game Gear, SG-1000, Atari 2600, ColecoVision, MSX), memoryCard (PlayStation, Neo Geo) and mouse (Nintendo 64). The keyboard of an MSX or a ZX Spectrum is part of the machine and is not chosen here.
texts.setting.port2.about: What is plugged into the second controller port. 'default' is the device this machine normally has there, and 'none' leaves the port empty. Each of the other choices exists on certain machines only, and choosing one on a machine that does not have it is refused. They are arcadeStick (Neo Geo), controlPad (Mega Drive), controller (Atari 5200), digitalGamepad (PlayStation), ePSM (NES), gamepad (Nintendo 64, NES, Master System, Game Gear, SG-1000, Atari 2600, ColecoVision, MSX), memoryCard (PlayStation, Neo Geo) and mouse (Nintendo 64). The keyboard of an MSX or a ZX Spectrum is part of the machine and is not chosen here.
texts.setting.port3.about: What is plugged into the third controller port. 'default' is the device this machine normally has there, and 'none' leaves the port empty. Each of the other choices exists on certain machines only, and choosing one on a machine that does not have it is refused. They are arcadeStick (Neo Geo), controlPad (Mega Drive), controller (Atari 5200), digitalGamepad (PlayStation), ePSM (NES), gamepad (Nintendo 64, NES, Master System, Game Gear, SG-1000, Atari 2600, ColecoVision, MSX), memoryCard (PlayStation, Neo Geo) and mouse (Nintendo 64). The keyboard of an MSX or a ZX Spectrum is part of the machine and is not chosen here.
texts.setting.port4.about: What is plugged into the fourth controller port. 'default' is the device this machine normally has there, and 'none' leaves the port empty. Each of the other choices exists on certain machines only, and choosing one on a machine that does not have it is refused. They are arcadeStick (Neo Geo), controlPad (Mega Drive), controller (Atari 5200), digitalGamepad (PlayStation), ePSM (NES), gamepad (Nintendo 64, NES, Master System, Game Gear, SG-1000, Atari 2600, ColecoVision, MSX), memoryCard (PlayStation, Neo Geo) and mouse (Nintendo 64). The keyboard of an MSX or a ZX Spectrum is part of the machine and is not chosen here.
texts.setting.region.about: Whether the console is an NTSC or a PAL model. The two differ in video timing and in the boot ROM, so a movie made on one does not play back on the other. Changing it restarts the core.
texts.slot.rom.help: The game the machine loads. For most machines this is a cartridge. The PlayStation takes a .cue file, the ZX Spectrum a .tzx or .tape file and the Neo Geo a .zip romset. Only the kinds that fit the chosen machine are offered. A Nintendo 64 cartridge can be in any of its three byte orders (.z64, .n64 or .v64) and the core works out which one it is. A PlayStation and an MSX can start with nothing here. The PlayStation then shows its BIOS menu and the MSX starts its BASIC. Every other machine needs a game and says so when there is none. Some machines also need their console BIOS, which is asked for on another page. The Nintendo 64 needs none.
texts.slot.savedata.help: The saved game that a cartridge with a battery starts with. This is the file that Emulator > Export Save Data... writes (EEPROM, SRAM or Flash, whichever the cartridge has, named save.eeprom, save.ram or save.flash as ares names them; a .eep, .fla, .sav or .srm of the same bytes is taken too). Put it here to continue a run from where another one stopped. It must be the size of the cartridge's save chip, and is in the byte order ares writes its own save files in (as Export Save Data writes it). The file is never changed. The project and the movie record exactly which file it was, so a movie that starts from a saved game can be played back by anyone who has the same file. Only the Nintendo 64 exports and loads its saves this way so far. A Nintendo 64DD game saves on its disk instead: Export Save Data hands out the disk it wrote to, and that disk goes in the game slot of a new project. The other machines keep their saves inside the savestate. A cartridge with no save memory keeps nothing, and the project says so. Leave this empty to start with a fresh cartridge.
texts.slot.subcart.help: Some Super Famicom cartridges have a slot of their own, and this is the cartridge that goes into it. A Satellaview memory pack (.bs) goes into the BS-X cartridge. Choose the BS-X as the game above and the pack here. A Sufami Turbo minicart (.st) goes into the Sufami Turbo cartridge (a second one goes into its slot B, for the games that link two), and a Game Boy cartridge goes into a Super Game Boy. The core finds the right slot from the file itself. Leave this empty for an ordinary cartridge, which is almost every game. A game that has no such slot reports an error when a file is given here.
